title: TB2-06566
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of the Slovak Republic (Slovakia) and claims refugee protection pursuant to ss. 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 ALLEGATIONS
The claimant fears persecution at the hands of the skinheads.
The claimant alleges that he was threatened and assaulted by the agents of persecution on account of his Roma ethnicity.
The panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
The claimant's identity is established through his oral testimony and the supporting documentation2 filed. Credibility
The claimant filed his original Personal Information Form (PIF) in June 2012 and filed an amendment to his narrative in March 2013.

In his oral testimony, the claimant stated that while he attended the first grade he was attacked by some of his fellow students. He stated that he did not report this incident to the police because he had been threatened by the assailants if they found out that he had reported them.

About three months after this assault, the claimant stated that he was assaulted again. This time he and his parents reported the matter to the teacher and the principal and the situation calmed down. He stated that he experienced no other assaults at this school after he had reported the matter to the school authorities.

The claimant stated that in 2005, when he was a high school student, he was assaulted by three skinheads. He reported the incident to the teacher who refused to intervene. Because he had suffered bruises as a result of the incident he attended at a physician's office who gave him a cream for his injuries but refused to give him a medical report. He stated that he tried to file a police report but the police would not accept a denunciation without a report from the doctor.

The claimant then stated that while in his second year of high school he was again assaulted by the agents of persecution. As a result of the assault he suffered bleeding from his head. He was taken to a doctor who treated him for his injuries but, once again, refused to give him a medical report. The claimant stated that, as with the previous assault, he was not able to file a denunciation with the authorities because he did not have a medical report.

The panel pointed out to the claimant that all of these assaults which he alleges he experienced at school had not been mentioned by him in his original PIF narrative and the panel asked him to explain the omission. He replied that at that time he did not know what needed to be included.

I reject this explanation. The claimant in his oral testimony outlined four different occasions when he alleges that he was assaulted by the agents of persecution at school. Even if he would not have provided the details of each assault in his narrative it is reasonable that he would have at least mentioned that during his school years the agents of persecution had assaulted him. The omission is an important fact in the claimant's story for it demonstrates at what early stage in his life he began to experience difficulties at the hands of the agents of persecution. The new information in his oral testimony amounts to omissions regarding significant aspects that go directly to the heart of the claimant's claim.3 It is reasonable to expect the claimant to have remembered this fact when writing his narrative. The claimant provided no reasonable explanation for this omission. I find on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant was not assaulted during his school years by the agents of persecution. The Immigration and Refugee Board (Board) has been upheld when rejecting major evidence which has been omitted from the PIF.4

The claimant then stated that in XXXX of 2009 while shopping, he was again assaulted by the agents of persecution who cut his back. As a result of the injury to his back, the claimant experienced problems with his kidney requiring surgery.

The claimant stated that the original doctor who treated him did not provide him with a medical report. Although he tried to file a report with the police, as with other occasions the police refused to take a complaint because he did not have a medical report. The panel asked him if he had returned to the police to file a report after he had undergone his surgery and he replied that he did but because the report did not indicate that the agents of persecution were responsible for the assault the police did not file a report.

The panel pointed out to the claimant that this particular incident, including the details of the injuries which he suffered, and the fact that he tried to file a police report, were not mentioned by him in his original narrative and the panel asked him to explain the omission. The claimant replied that he wanted to be concise. I reject this explanation. This is not a question of being concise about a fact which the claimant mentioned in his narrative. This is a question of the fact that the claimant failed to make any mention of this particular assault in his narrative. The omission is an important fact in the claimant's story for it demonstrates the severity of the injuries which the claimant suffered as a result of this assault. The new information in his oral testimony amounts to omissions regarding significant aspects that go directly to the heart of the claimant's claim.5 It is reasonable to expect the claimant to have remembered this fact when writing his narrative. The claimant provided no reasonable explanation for this omission. I find on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant was not assaulted in XXXX of 2009 by the agents of persecution. The Board has been upheld when rejecting major evidence which has been omitted from the PIF.6

The claimant then stated that in XXXX 2011 he was again attacked by three skinheads. As with the other assaults the claimant alleges that he was treated by a doctor after the assault but the doctor refused to provide him with a medical report and because of that the police would not take a report of the assault.

The panel pointed out to the claimant that he had not mentioned this assault in his original narrative and he replied that he did not have a clue as to what to include in his original narrative. I reject this explanation. The original narrative does make mention of at least one assault. It is reasonable that the claimant would have also remembered this particular assault in his original narrative for it demonstrates the frequency of the assaults which he suffered at the hands of the agents of persecution. The new information in his oral testimony amounts to omissions regarding significant aspects that go directly to the heart of the claimant's claim.7 It is reasonable to expect the claimant to have remembered this fact when writing his narrative. The claimant provided no reasonable explanation for this omission. I find on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant was not assaulted in XXXX 2011 by the agents of persecution. The Board has been upheld when rejecting major evidence which has been omitted from the PIF.8

The claimant then stated that in XXXX 2012 he was assaulted by four skinheads. As a result of the injuries he was bleeding in the head and suffered bruises. As with all previous assaults the attending doctor refused to issue a medical report and because of this the claimant could not file a report with the police.

The panel pointed out to the claimant that the panel has heard a large number of refugee claims from the Slovak Republic where medical reports from either individual physicians or state health institutions were submitted along with the claims. The claimant replied that he did not believe me that medical reports had been submitted to me by refugee claimants from the Slovak Republic. The panel also mentioned to the claimant that the Board's documentation with respect to the Slovak Republic does not mention that the police would not file a report if a medical certificate was not presented. The panel pointed out to the claimant that if what he was saying were true, some independent international organization or NGO would make mention of the fact that in the Slovak Republic the police does not issue reports unless they have a medical report of the incident. The claimant replied that human rights are being violated.

I reject this explanation. It is reasonable to expect that reports of organizations who comment on the difficulties experienced by the Romas in the Slovak Republic would make mention of the fact that, one of the difficulties which they experience, is that the police do not issue a police report if there is no medical report on the assault. If what the claimant alleges is true, it is reasonable to expect that international organizations who write reports on the state of the Romas in the Slovak Republic would have made mention of this fact. There is no documentary proof to back up the claimant's allegations.
I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant was not assaulted in XXXX 2012. State Protection

I find, on a balance of probabilities that the principal claimant has not established that state protection is unavailable for him in the Slovak Republic. There is a presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens. The claimant may rebut this presumption by providing "clear and convincing" proof of lack of state protection in their country of origin. The claimant must approach his or her state for protection, providing state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.9

Evidence that protection being offered is not necessarily perfect10 is not clear and convincing proof of the state's inability to protect its citizens, as no government can guarantee the protection of all its citizens at all times. However, where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authority in place, and makes serious efforts to protect its citizens, the mere fact it is not always successful at doing so will not be enough to justify a claim that the victims are unable to avail themselves of protection.11 The onus is on the claimant to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that state protection is inadequate.12

The burden of proving an absence of state protection is directly proportional to the level of democracy that exists in the state.13 The documentary evidence before the Board indicates the Slovak Republic is a functioning democracy.14 It has functioning political and judicial systems in place and an official apparatus sufficient to provide a measure of protection to its citizens. Local failures to provide effective policing do not amount to a lack of state protection unless they are part of a pattern of state's inability or refusal to provide protection.15 Therefore, a claimant must do more than approach one police officer unsuccessfully before deciding that state protection would not be forthcoming. There is an onus on the claimant to exhaust all courses of action reasonably available to him.16

The Slovak Republic is in control of its territory and has functioning security forces, both military and police, in place. There is no evidence of a total breakdown of state authority in the country. Therefore, the burden of attempting to show that one should not be required to exhaust all avenues of domestic recourse is a heavy one.17 The Slovak Republic security forces are hierarchical and allow a person to complain to a higher authority, particularly the Bureau for the Inspection Service of the Police Corps, if dissatisfied with the services provided.18
In this particular claim, I have made a credibility finding with respect to all of the alleged assaults suffered by the claimant.
I find that there is state protection for members of the Roma community in the Slovak Republic.

The documentary evidence of the Board19 and counsel's documents20 do indicate that Roma and other minorities suffer discrimination and violence in the Slovak Republic and that police mistreat Romani suspects and detainees. I have reviewed counsel's documents, including the video. The evidence also supports the claimant's contention that organized neo-Nazi groups and sympathizers harass and attack minorities including the Roma. Further, police might not intervene or investigate properly when there are Roma involved, although this varies by jurisdiction. The Roma generally face discrimination in health care, education, housing and employment in the Slovak Republic as well.21 Many Roma face severe difficulties and discrimination accessing adequate housing and employment and they experience segregation in schools and health care facilities.22

However, the documentary evidence indicates that the Slovak Republic has taken, and is taking, steps to combat these deficiencies and there are signs of real progress. For example, there is a deeply entrenched legal framework as a basis from which the Slovak Republic can combat these problems. The legal framework includes the Constitution, legislation and international obligations as well.

I note that the government has taken proactive steps to address the issues of discrimination and violence targeting minorities, in particular the Roma. Sources provide the 2009 example in which police officers in Košice detained six Romani boys, forced them to strip, hit and kiss each other, threatened them with loaded guns, unleashed police dogs on them, and yelled anti-Roma statements at them (ERRC Mar. 2011, 28; Council of Europe Feb. 2012, 77). Six police officers and four senior officials were reportedly dismissed following the incident (ibid.). The ERRC states that three officers were still employed by the police force at the time of the first court hearing on 26 August 2010 (Mar. 2011, 28). The court case against the police officers involved in the incident was reportedly pending at the end of 2011 (AI 2012; US 24 May 2012, 2).23 The National Roma Integration Strategy up to 2020 was adopted by the government in January 2012, in accordance with its obligations as a member of the EU, and focuses on four main areas: education, employment, healthcare, and housing (UN 24 May 2012). According to the government, the goals of the strategy are "to halt the segregation of Roma communities; to facilitate a significant positive turn in the social inclusion of Roma communities; to foster non-discrimination; and to change the attitude of the majority population toward the Roma minority" (Slovak Republic [2011]). Sources indicate that Roma communities were consulted throughout the development process of the strategy (OSF 14 June 2012; UN 24 May 2012). According to the OSF representative, the integration strategy is a "great" policy with "concrete measures, financial commitments, and time frames" (14 June 2012). According to the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the strategy includes a regular monitoring mechanism (UN 24 May 2012). In correspondence with the Research Directorate, an official at the Embassy of the Slovak Republic in Ottawa indicated that as a member of the Decade of Roma Inclusion 2005-2015, the Slovak Republic regularly submits progress reports (Slovak Republic 13 June 2012).24

Slovakia's Anti-Discrimination Act (Act), which was adopted in 2004, prohibits direct and indirect discrimination on the grounds of race, nationality, ethnic origin, among others, in the fields of education, social security, employment, healthcare, and access to goods and services. According to the Council of Europe, the Act is "largely under-implemented" due to inadequate awareness of discrimination of the Act among the legal profession, lengthy court proceedings, and a "reported reluctance to [grant] meaningful compensation."25

The objective evidence makes clear that the authorities in Slovakia have taken a plethora of measures to mitigate the discrimination faced by the Roma. The government has funded education, health care, employment and improved living conditions for the Roma. Slovakia pays appropriate attention to the social inclusion of Roma. Support of social inclusion of persons endangered by social exclusion or socially excluded persons through the development of services with special focus on marginalized Roma communities is among priorities of the Operational Programme Employment and Social Inclusion (2007-2013). Despite these efforts by the Slovak Republic government, statistics indicate that Roma are still underemployed and less educated. The government has set objectives focused on the improvement of access to work opportunities with particular emphasis on non-discriminatory access to the labour market as well as on active policies and programmes directed to the labour market, education, continuing education, and the support of self-employment activities.

I note that the information is mixed as it relates to the Roma in Slovakia, there are problems in certain areas including in the election of an anti-Roma governor, the violence by extremists and other violent entities that specifically target Romas and other minorities. Overall I find there is evidence of a concrete action taken on the part of the police to offer protection to the Roma and other minorities.

Despite the negative reporting, the documentary evidence reveals that the state does not condone or acquiesce in the racial and discriminatory behaviour, particularly at the hands of extremists and/or skinheads.

There are legitimate concerns from some groups that there is impunity for racially motivated attacks and the police responses are not sufficient; however, the preponderance of evidence indicates that the state is taking action against extremists and does not condone or assent to extremist actions. I note there is also some evidence that at the operational level the state is taking action to address the discrimination and violence targeting the Roma population. Despite these efforts by the Slovak government, statistics indicate that Roma are still underemployed and less educated. Critics claim these programs do not go far enough or are just superficial. Even so, I find the preponderance of evidence is that there are programs in place resulting in improvements to the lives of Roma.

The above-noted examples indicate that, on the whole, the Slovak Republic has undertaken significant efforts to provide better protection for its citizens and is making serious effort to combat corruption.

Documentary evidence states that citizens have the right to lodge complaints against the unlawful conduct of police officers. European Partners Against Corruption (EPAC), a network of European national police oversight bodies and anti-corruption authorities indicates that the Section of Control and Inspection Services (of the Ministry of the Interior) has investigative, supervisory and inspection tasks related to disciplinary matters, criminal matters and service regulation. The Ministry of the Interior states that the section of Control and Inspection Services is a "separate unit" of the Ministry which is "independent from the management and structures of the police" and subordinated to the Ministry of the Interior. However, several sources question the degree of independence of the section. Complaints are investigated by a police force investigator. A representative of the Slovak Republic's Office of the Public Defender of Rights, or the ombudsman's office, indicated that their office does have the jurisdiction to review cases related to police procedures or inactivity. According to the United States Department of State, Country Reports 2011, authorities charged 122 police officers with 167 crimes in 2010. Disciplinary actions ranged from fines to removing officers from the police force. There were 47 cases of "abuse of power," 11 cases of corruption and seven cases of obstruction of justice. Other charges reportedly included battery, assault and battery and illegal intrusion into homes.26

The documentary evidence indicates that police service may vary depending on the jurisdiction but the Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe (COE) reported that police response to racially motivated crimes has improved although it continues to face challenges. The COE credits this improvement to the Slovak Republic's establishment of a Commission for Co-ordinating Actions to Eliminate Racially Motivated Crime, which is tasked with sharing information on racially motivated crime and eliminating racial discrimination, including police mistreatment. The Slovak Republic has implemented an outreach initiative consisting of 231 "Police Roma specialists" who spend 70 percent of their time in Roma communities to build trust. The Commissioner of Human Rights stated that 120 police officers have been trained on "policing in a multiethnic environment," particularly Roma areas, and noted that the government has committed to recruiting Roma police officers to the national police force and to the municipal police.27

Police do take action when they are requested to do so and that state does prosecute. Investigation of racially motivated attacks against Roma in 2011 varied by jurisdiction, but also states that several people were detained for racially motivated attacks. The Slovak Republic government is reportedly implementing a plan that includes a special police unit in charge of monitoring extremist activities.28 There is documentary evidence that indicates that some police officers are biased against Roma, particularly in Eastern Slovakia and in rural areas and they may ignore complaints or fail to adequately deal with incidents against Roma. Further, only a limited number of perpetrators are successfully prosecuted in cases of violence against Roma, and even fewer receive prison sentences.29

The documentary evidence indicates the Slovak Republic has implemented an outreach initiative consisting of 231 "Police Roma specialists" who spend 70 percent of their time in Roma communities to build trust.30 The Commissioner of Human Rights stated that 120 police officers have been trained on "policing in a multiethnic environment," particularly Roma areas, and noted that the government has committed to recruiting Roma police officers to the national police force and to the municipal police.31

In terms of discrimination in employment, employees may protect their rights not only with their employer, but also through the intermediary of employee representatives, labour inspectorates, or the court if they consider themselves affected by failure to apply the principle of equal treatment. They may further demand that the entity that failed to apply the principle of equal treatment refrains from such conduct and, where possible, rectifies the unlawful situation or provides adequate satisfaction. In cases where the employer violates the principle of equal treatment with regard to access to employment, the applicant has the right to seek adequate pecuniary compensation by filing a claim with the court. With respect to education, right to education in a national minority language is enshrined in the Constitution. The national project on "Improving the qualification potential of the Roma community by introducing a new course on Roma studies in the system of secondary schools" was carried out under the professional guidance of the National Institute for Education was aimed at eliminating the limited access of the Roma to education and employment due to the language barrier, cultural handicaps, low mobility, and social and economic situation of families and raising educational attainment of the Roma in the Slovak Republic as a basic prerequisite for their participation in the labour market and integration into society in general.

Further, the Constitution guarantees the right of the citizens belonging to national minorities to create and maintain their educational institutions. The teaching of the languages of national minorities is provided also in state-run institutions of higher education. These schools are part of the Slovak Republic's system of education and instruction and are financed from the state budget. Education and instruction of children and pupils from socially disadvantaged environment is carried out in schools under this Act using specific methods and forms to meet the needs of these disadvantaged students. The state employs compulsory education for all students. There are subsidies on food, school materials and subsidy on motivational allowance for children attending preschool facilities or schools and living in families that receive benefits and allowances or whose income does not exceed the level of subsistence minimum. Under these programs school attendance of pupils has improved but educational attainment of pupils from socially disadvantaged environment has not improved.

The evidence clearly shows that the Roma still suffer from higher rates of unemployment and lower educational achievement. The Roma are still excluded from regular life in terms of housing and health care. However, the documentary evidence indicates that the state is making serious efforts and although progress is slow, there are signs of progress. It is unreasonable to expect that these measures should have prevented or eliminated all racism or acts of violence related to race. However, this is an indication of the serious efforts the state has made to combat racial discrimination in every aspect of society. The progress is not as rapid and there have been set-backs and obstacles, but the commitment of the state to continue the battle is not in question. The quality of existence for the Roma is not what it should be, but their existence is not threatened by the state. While skinheads and extremists seek to threaten the existence of the Roma, the state takes serious actions against that as well.

There is information in the documentation to indicate that bribery and corruption remain issues in Slovakian security forces. However, weighted against this is persuasive evidence that indicates the Slovak Republic candidly acknowledges its past problems and is making serious efforts to rectify the corruption and impunity that exists.

The preponderance of the objective evidence regarding current country conditions suggests that, although not perfect, there is adequate state protection in the Slovak Republic for victims of crime, that the Slovak Republic is making serious efforts to address the problems of criminality, and that the police are both willing and able to protect victims. Police corruption and deficiencies, although existing and noted by the Board, are not systemic. I am of the view in canvassing the documentary evidence, that, as a whole, the issues of corruption and deficiencies are being addressed by the Slovak Republic.

Further documentary evidence indicates the following:32 Sources indicated that corruption in the Slovak police and judiciary system is an ongoing problem as there were reports of corruption and misconduct in the police forces. For instance, police corruption at the border "may have hampered" efforts to reduce human smuggling.

For the year 2005, Transparency International (TI) puts Slovakia at the 47th rank out of 158 evaluated countries ranked from the least to the most corrupt. TI stated that Slovakia was among the countries to improve the most in comparison with the previous year.

In 1999, a program of judicial reforms that increased state action against corruption began. According to Country Reports 2004, 90 per cent of the Slovak Republic's "Government Action Plan to Fight Corruption" was implemented at year's end. However, a European Union (EU) summary of legislation stated that "Slovakia must pursue its efforts to implement its national programme of action."

As well, although the United States' International Narcotics Control Strategy Report 2005 reported that, "Slovakia has made major legislative strides in the fight against corruption" it also indicated that the execution of the new measures "remain[ed] a challenge."

The Slovak government created its "Anti-Corruption Department" in December 2002 and put it in charge of applying its national anti-corruption program. This department develops policy, concepts and programs, and proposes laws on combating corruption. It also monitors information on corruption and advances its own projects to reduce corruption.

The International Narcotics Control Strategy Report 2005 provided a comprehensive description of the recent state measures put forward in the fight against corruption: Officials serious about creating transparent rules and prosecuting abuses have been put in key positions, a new conflict of interest law passed in 2004, and a special prosecutor and court to fight corruption were set up. The head of the [Government of Slovakia] anticorruption office is a noted human rights lawyer who encourages the use of "sting" operations and introduced a "whistle blower" statute to protect government employees who talk to investigators about corruption in their offices.

The Slovak government indicated that the special court for the prosecution of corruption crimes with nationwide jurisdiction was to be established in Bratislava and was to be operational in September 2004. In November 2005, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) confirmed that the Special Court and prosecutor had started their work and that they had "exclusive jurisdiction over domestic and foreign bribery."

The justice minister of Slovakia recognized that confidence in the Slovak justice system was "low." He stated, however, that a reform through which judges are assigned cases randomly had helped to "improv[e] transparency in the judicial system." Country Reports 2004 added that the computerized system assigning cases was implemented at almost all court levels.

As well, a program which permits plea bargaining with people who have inside information about organized crime and "the legalization of the use of undercover agents" in the fight against corruption was also put forward.

Laws regulating professional codes of conduct were amended to make sure that the principle of "zero tolerance" would be applied in cases of corruption. Another legislative change, criminalizing "failure to disclose corruption," was implemented in December 2003. Freedom House added that the Law on Free Access to Information increased transparency.

In May 2004, the appointed "special prosecutor to fight corruption" brought charges against the mayor of Bratislava-Raca, who was suspected of accepting a bribe, and referred other cases to an anticorruption court.

Over the year 2004, the director of the "alien detention facility" was arrested as a suspect in human smuggling and "several corruption charges" were pressed against members of the customs and immigration police.

The claimant has not established that were he to return to the Slovak Republic today, state protection would not be reasonably forthcoming or that it is objectively unreasonable for him to seek that protection.

I find that the claimant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, there is inadequate state protection for him in the Slovak Republic. I find the claimant has failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence and his claim fails under sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA.
I therefore determine that claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

The Refugee Protection Division therefore rejects his claim.
